'''Edgerrin Tyree James''' ({{IPAc-en|ˈ|ɛ|dʒ|ər|ɪ|n}}; born August 1, 1978) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 11 seasons. He played [[college football]] at the [[University of Miami]] for the [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami Hurricanes]]. He was selected by the [[Indianapolis Colts]] fourth overall in the [[1999 NFL draft]]. James also played for the [[Arizona Cardinals]] and [[Seattle Seahawks]].

He was named [[National Football League Rookie of the Year Award|AP NFL Offensive Rookie of the Year]] in 1999 and earned four [[Pro Bowl]] selections and three [[All-Pro]] selections. James is the Colts' all-time leader in career rushing yards, and attempts. James is 14th on the all-time rushing list, and a member of the [[List of National Football League career rushing yards leaders|10,000 Yards rushing club]]. He was elected to the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] as a member of the Class of 2020.<ref>{{cite news |last=Legwold |first=Jeff |date=1 February 2020 |title=Steelers' Troy Polamalu, Colts' Edgerrin James elected to Hall of Fame |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/28614718/steelers-troy-polamalu-colts-edgerrin-james-elected-hall-fame |work=ESPN |access-date=2 February 2020}}</ref>

{{Short description|American football player (born 1951)}} {{Use American English|date=April 2025}} {{Use mdy dates|date=June 2024}} {{Infobox NFL biography | name = Eddie Payton | image = | image_size = | alt = | caption = | number = 26, 34, 31 | position = [[Return specialist]],
[[Running back]] | birth_date = {{birth date and age|1951|8|3}} | birth_place = [[Columbia, Mississippi]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | height_ft = 5 | height_in = 8 | weight_lbs = 175 | high_school = | college = [[Jackson State Tigers football|Jackson State]] | undraftedyear = 1973 | pastteams = * [[Cleveland Browns]] ({{NFL Year|1977}}) * [[Detroit Lions]] ({{NFL Year|1977}}) * [[Kansas City Chiefs]] ({{NFL Year|1978}}) * [[Toronto Argonauts]] ({{CFL Year|1979}}) * [[Minnesota Vikings]] ({{NFL Year|1980|1982}}) | statleague = NFL | statlabel1 = [[Return yards]] | statvalue1 = 5,063 | statlabel2 = [[Touchdown|Return touchdowns]] | statvalue2 = 3 | statlabel3 = Rush attempts | statvalue3 = 6 | statlabel4 = [[Rushing yards]] | statvalue4 = 28 | statlabel5 = Rushing touchdowns | statvalue5 = }} '''Edward Charles Payton Jr.''' (born August 3, 1951) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] player who was a [[running back]] and [[kick returner]] for five seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 1977 to 1982 for the [[Cleveland Browns]], [[Detroit Lions]], [[Kansas City Chiefs]] and [[Minnesota Vikings]]. He also played in the [[Canadian Football League]] for the Toronto Argonauts in 1979 but was released after playing 2 games. He is the older brother of the late [[Chicago Bears]] player [[Walter Payton]], the uncle of Brittney Payton and the uncle of the current [[WGN-TV]] sports anchor [[Jarrett Payton]]. Payton played [[college football]] for the [[Jackson State Tigers football|Jackson State Tigers]] and signed undrafted by the Browns. Payton was primarily used as a kick and punt returner. He led the NFL with 53 kickoffs for 1184 yards in 1980. Payton ran back two kickoffs and one punt return for [[touchdown]]s in his career, two in the same game. On December 17, 1977, Payton ran a kick return and a punt return for a touchdown for the Lions in a game against the Vikings. Eddie Payton is the former head [[golf]] coach at Jackson State,[https://www.espn.com/page2/tvlistings/show64transcript.html Outside the Lines: 1... And Only] ESPN, Retrieved on 2006-12-03. coaching both the men's and women's teams. From 1986 – 2016, Payton led the Jackson State Golf program to 37 Southwestern Athletic Conference championships. His men's team won 23 conference titles, 8 National Minority championships, and was the first HBCU to make the NCAA Men's National Golf Championships in 1995. He helped start the women's golf program in 1994. From there, he led the women's team to 14 SWAC titles and also the first HBCU NCAA appearance for women in 1999.
